audits.title: Use of Two Pain Assessment Tools to Improve Pain Recognition in Post Stroke Patients: A Quality Improvement Project
audits.standard: Formal pain assessment documented on admission in post-stroke patients

cycle1.result: Only 25% of patients had formal pain assessment documented on admission.

audits.intervention: Pain assessment proforma incorporated into the admission proforma, with the Numerical Pain Scale and the Abbey Pain Scale.
audits.other_findings: Staff found the proforma a useful prompt; barriers were time constraints, unfamiliarity with tools and possible inaccuracy of scores.
audits.citation: Seebah S, Fan C. Use of Two Pain Assessment Tools to Improve Pain Recognition in Post Stroke Patients: A Quality Improvement Project. Age and Ageing. 2024;53(Supplement_4). doi:10.1093/ageing/afae178.252.

audits.title: The assessment of pain: an audit of physiotherapy practice.
audits.standard: Recording of pain assessment and reassessment using quantified methods
audits.setting: Four hospital physiotherapy departments in England

cycle1.result: Pain reassessment not recorded in 29%; quantified methods used in 21% of initial assessments and less than 2% of reassessments.

audits.other_findings: Quantified pain measurement was not standard physiotherapy practice.
audits.citation: Turner P, Whitfield A, Brewster S, Halligan M, Kennedy J. The assessment of pain: an audit of physiotherapy practice. Aust J Physiother. 1996;42(1):55-62. doi:10.1016/s0004-9514(14)60441-4. PMID: 11676636.

audits.title: Using quality improvement strategies to enhance pediatric pain assessment.
audits.standard: Pain assessment guidelines; American Pain Society quality assurance guidelines
audits.setting: Paediatric haematology/oncology unit, Children's Hospital Oakland

cycle1.result: Baseline satisfaction and documentation compliance measured; figures not given.

audits.intervention: Staff education on paediatric pain assessment tools and a standardised pain assessment protocol.

cycle2.result: Increased pain assessment and satisfaction; increased compliance with guidelines confirmed by chart audit.

audits.other_findings: Staff sample 68 at time 1 and 82 at time 2.
audits.citation: Treadwell MJ, Franck LS, Vichinsky E. Using quality improvement strategies to enhance pediatric pain assessment. Int J Qual Health Care. 2002;14(1):39-47. doi:10.1093/intqhc/14.1.39. PMID: 11871628.

audits.title: Using quality improvement to address pain management practices in nursing homes.
audits.standard: Pain quality indicators for assessment and treatment

cycle1.result: 8% of residents in pain had pain assessments; 31% received non-pharmacological treatment.

audits.intervention: Feedback on pain quality indicator data, pain management education and technical assistance with Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles.
audits.other_findings: Pain medication use did not change.
audits.citation: Horner JK, Hanson LC, Wood D, Silver AG, Reynolds KS. Using quality improvement to address pain management practices in nursing homes. J Pain Symptom Manage. 2005;30(3):271-277. doi:10.1016/j.jpainsymman.2005.03.014. PMID: 16183011.

audits.title: Measuring the "fifth vital sign" in cataract surgery patients--is it necessary?
audits.standard: Hospital pain assessment policy; compliance target 85%
audits.setting: Outpatient cataract surgery, Wilmer Eye Institute, Johns Hopkins Hospital
audits.intervention: Staff education and changes to the critical pathway.
audits.other_findings: Earlier review of 135 patients found 21% reported pain and no nurse pain reassessment in 62%.
audits.citation: Henry C, Navarro V, Jun A, Annaberdyev S. Measuring the "fifth vital sign" in cataract surgery patients--is it necessary?. Insight. 2006;31(2):7-9. PMID: 17253012.

audits.title: Are we providing the best possible pain management for our elderly patients in the acute-care setting?
audits.standard: Relevant pain management standards of practice (not specified)

cycle1.result: 78% had a documented pain assessment in previous 24 h, but 83% of these were only a general comment; 62% had no analgesia 1 h before mobilising or significant dressing.

audits.intervention: Education sessions and introduction of the Abbey Pain Scale.

cycle2.result: Increased staff awareness; Abbey Pain Scale used well and prompted pain assessment (figures not given).

audits.citation: McLiesh P, Mungall D, Wiechula R. Are we providing the best possible pain management for our elderly patients in the acute-care setting?. Int J Evid Based Healthc. 2009;7(3):173-180. doi:10.1111/j.1744-1609.2009.00138.x. PMID: 21631858.

audits.title: PA1 An internal audit into the adequacy of pain assessment in a hospice setting.
audits.standard: SOCRATES mnemonic pain assessment; target 100% fully assessed with all eight elements; regular and breakthrough analgesia prescribed

cycle1.result: 0% fully assessed with all SOCRATES elements; 66.7% partially assessed; mean 3.3 elements used; regular and breakthrough analgesia prescribed for 100%

audits.other_findings: Hospice met the analgesia prescribing standard but fell well short on full pain assessment.
audits.citation: Manna A, Sarkar SK, Khanra LK. PA1 An internal audit into the adequacy of pain assessment in a hospice setting. BMJ Support Palliat Care. 2015;5 Suppl 1:A19-20. doi:10.1136/bmjspcare-2015-000906.61. PMID: 25960483.

audits.title: Knowledge translation and process improvement interventions increased pain assessment documentation in a large quaternary paediatric post-anaesthesia care unit.
audits.standard: Documented pain assessment (pain intensity score with validated measure) during PACU stay; no target stated
audits.setting: Post-anaesthesia care unit, large quaternary university-affiliated paediatric hospital (Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto)

cycle1.result: 69% of charts had at least one documented pain assessment.

audits.intervention: PDSA: PACU flowsheets modified; knowledge translation strategy with educational meetings, huddle discussions, reminders (screensavers, posters, emails) and audit feedback.

cycle2.result: >90% at 4 and 5 months and 100% at 6 months.

audits.other_findings: Further work needed on monitoring moderate to severe pain.
audits.citation: Stocki D, McDonnell C, Wong G, Kotzer G, Shackell K, Campbell F. Knowledge translation and process improvement interventions increased pain assessment documentation in a large quaternary paediatric post-anaesthesia care unit. BMJ Open Qual. 2018;7(3):e000319. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2018-000319. PMID: 30167475.

audits.title: Using the Model for Improvement to implement the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool in an adult intensive care unit.
audits.standard: Pain assessed and documented at least every four hours and CPOT score ≥3 treated with rescue opioid bolus
audits.setting: Intensive Care Unit, Raigmore Hospital, NHS Highland, Inverness

cycle1.result: Only 30% of Scottish ICUs using validated behavioural pain tools (April 2017 telephone audit).

audits.intervention: Implementation of the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool using the Model for Improvement over six months.

cycle2.result: Four-hourly pain assessments increased to 89% and treatment of CPOT scores ≥3 to 100%.

audits.citation: Mascarenhas M, Beattie M, Roxburgh M, MacKintosh J, Clarke N, Srivastava D. Using the Model for Improvement to implement the Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool in an adult intensive care unit. BMJ Open Qual. 2018;7(4):e000304. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2017-000304. PMID: 30515466.

audits.title: Improving Pain Reassessment and Documentation Rates: A Quality Improvement Project in a Teaching Hospital's Emergency Department.
audits.setting: Community teaching hospital emergency department (St. Margaret Hospital)

cycle1.result: Pain score reassessment and documentation rate 36.2% (CI 30.3%-42.3%).

audits.intervention: Nurse focus groups, daily audits of individual nurses' pain reassessment and a weekly newsletter reporting rates.

audits.title: A prospective audit project into the adequacy of pain assessment in the medical and surgical wards in a North London District General Hospital.
audits.standard: Royal College of Anaesthetists standards for pain assessment (pain score documented as the fifth vital sign)
audits.setting: Medical and surgical wards, North London district general hospital (Whittington Hospital)

cycle1.result: 29 (14%) had no pain score with their last observations; recorded scores did not match directly reported scores in 41% of medical and 71% of surgical patients; 20 (15%) medical and 26 (38%) surgical patients were in moderate to severe pain.

audits.other_findings: Analgesia provision differed between medical and surgical wards; an education programme was recommended.
audits.citation: Atkinson VJ, Almahdi B. A prospective audit project into the adequacy of pain assessment in the medical and surgical wards in a North London District General Hospital. Br J Pain. 2014;8(2):78-83. doi:10.1177/2049463713510288. PMID: 26516539.
